correctness.rationale: For n>=3, exactly five leader-pair cost classes are derived by eigenspace decomposition of the grounded Laplacian, with an at-most-four-dimensional quotient. The three noncontenders are proven strictly worse than the missing-endpoint pair by positive rational differences. The remaining difference has numerator f(n)=n^3-6n^2+5n-1 with values f(3)=f(4)=-13, f(5)=-1, f(6)=29 and first difference 3n(n-3)>0 for n>=4. The edge case n=3 is checked by the correct reduced quotient/direct inverse. A standalone SymPy program reconstructs all eight orbit identities and checks 245 direct rational grounded inverses (n=3..7). These finite comparisons corroborate the all-size algebraic proof.

originality.rationale: The known broad joint-centrality criterion for selecting noise-free leaders does not state or evaluate the five leader-pair orbits of a balanced biclique with one missing edge, nor the exact five-to-six switch. Inspected specialized results cover paths/cycles. Searches for alternative defective-biclique, pinned consensus and grounded-inverse-trace formulations did not reveal an implication that settles this optimizer classification. Priority outside the inspected corpus remains uncertain.
residual_risks: An unindexed or inaccessible primary paper may already contain an equivalent explicit defective-biclique classification.
General joint-centrality formulas apply to this graph after evaluation, so the originality attaches only to the new five-orbit ordering and exact phase boundary, not to the general objective.
No separate independent mathematical validation has been completed.

value.rationale: The exact optimizer transition is motivated by how one missing communication link alters stochastic-consensus leader choice in a dense two-community graph. It settles all sizes n>=3, all minimizers, multiplicities, and the full boundary, and it reverses the intact-graph same-part choice for n<=5. The non-obvious n=5 gap is 1/720, warranting exact arithmetic. This is a natural graph-fault design fact, not a renamed invariant, a selected numeric sample, or a generic matrix identity.
